citations.citation: "Green Tree Tavern." Chicagology. Transcribing the Inter Ocean of 1 July 1883 — the old-settlers hotel feature, in which named witnesses who had lived in the house are shown a sketch of it and asked to correct it — and Edwin O. Gale's Reminiscences of Early Chicago and Vicinity (1902), around nine city directories 1839-1885 and Chicago Tribune notices of the 1880 move and the 1902 collapse.

transcribes.note: Carries every Green Tree claim in this dataset: the function and occupants, the two-storey block with a divided hall and a stairway to the second floor, the gable with an attic window that fixes the roof form, and the dated span. Recollection by men who lived in the house, taken down in print — rung 2, not the reporter's rung.
transcribes.work: Inter Ocean, 'Old Chicago' — the early-hotels feature on the Green Tree: interviews with F. H. Taylor (in Chicago from 1834, lodged in the west one-storey addition), John Gray (landlord 1838-41) and Mrs. Murphy of the United States Hotel, each shown the S. W. Fallis sketch and asked to correct it

transcribes.note: Gale reached Chicago in 1835 and describes the bar-room from inside: the room module ('about 12x12, with two windows 6x8'), the whitewashed walls, ceilings and board partitions, and the seven-and-a-half-foot ceiling the record's storey height is reasoned from. A participant writing his own recollection — rung 2.

endings.text: Your list is crossed off and the load is packed. In this imagined departure you take the western road prepared, with what is left of the purse.
You set out light, with money in hand and gaps in the kit. In this imagined departure, the road will have to supply the rest.

evidence.locator: Inter Ocean, 1 July 1883, 'Old Chicago' early-hotels feature as transcribed by Chicagology; landlord chronology (Ingersoll, 1834–1837).
evidence.text: The Green Tree was a public house at Lake and West Water; the old settlers' account gives Chester Ingersoll as its landlord from 1834 to 1837.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 issue, Goss & Cobb advertisement headed 'Saddle & Harness Making', read from the scan.
evidence.text: Goss & Cobb advertised a saddle and harness shop at the corner of Lake and Canal streets, with saddles, harness, bridles, martingales and trunks, and repairs.

evidence.locator: 13 June 1835 issue: dissolution notice dated 'Chicago, Feb. 18, 1835' (claim c015) and Cobb's continuation card (claim c016).
evidence.text: The Goss & Cobb partnership was dissolved on 18 February 1835, and S. B. Cobb's card printed beside the notice says he will continue the business at his shop.

evidence.locator: 3 Dec 1833, p. 3, col. 4 (Peck's standing card, run to 10 Dec 1834); 2 July 1834, p. 4, col. 4 ('a full stock of fresh GOODS'). Transcription-mediated reading.
evidence.text: P. F. W. Peck advertised from the corner of LaSalle and South Water streets a stock of dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots and shoes, and hats.

evidence.locator: 26 Nov 1833 issue, advertisement headed 'Grocery & Provision Store. B. JONES.'; Andreas vol. 1, the 1834 advertisers' summary ('grocery and provision store and forwarding and commission store by H. Jones').
evidence.text: A Jones grocery and provision store advertised in 1833; Andreas lists the same trade with forwarding and commission among the 1834 advertisers. The ad reads 'B. Jones', Andreas 'H. Jones'.
Neither source gives the store's street or lot; its position on South Water Street is a reconstruction.

evidence.locator: Andreas, scan p. 1161, the Asahel Pierce paragraph (arrival, shop at Lake and Canal, Temple & Co. stage-line ironing, the 'Bull' plough).
evidence.text: Asahel Pierce arrived on 8 October 1833 and built a blacksmith shop on Lake Street at the corner of Canal; he ironed the first stage line between Chicago and St Louis in January 1834 and made 'Bull' ploughs from spring 1834.

evidence.reasoning: Uses the structure records' own scene-date phases: Ingersoll's tenancy spans 1835, Cobb's continuation card runs in June 1835, Peck's card runs to December 1834 and Pierce's shop is attested from 1833 with later enlargement. The Green Tree and Peck positions are inferred; Cobb's and Pierce's corner quadrant is not attested.
evidence.text: Each trade is carried to 1 July 1835 from evidence dated before it; none of the sources records a sale, a price or a customer on that day.

The visitor's westward errand, the fifteen-dollar purse, every price, the readiness count, the two endings and the Ready for the Road keepsake are invented connective narrative, not historical events or prices.

keepsake.text: A fictional supply list from five Chicago trades, crossed off for the road west.
keepsake.title: Ready for the Road

legs.note: A block west along Lake Street to the Canal Street crossing, where the saddlery's corner is attested and its quadrant is not.
legs.story: Before buying anything, decide how the load will travel.

legs.note: A few steps: Pierce's documented junction is the same Lake and Canal crossing.
legs.story: Harness and ironwork are seen to at the same corner.

legs.note: The long leg, and the only crossing: east over the South Branch to the commercial block on South Water Street.
legs.story: With the carrying settled, fill the load on the east bank.

opening.text: You are leaving Chicago for the prairie road west, with an imagined purse of fifteen dollars. Five exterior stops sell what the trip needs. The errand, the purse and every price are reconstructed; the trades are documented.

premise: Leave town with a practical kit, sound equipment and enough money for the road.

stops.narrative: Over an imagined table, set a short list: something to carry the load, a few tools, food for the road and sound ironwork.
stops.text: Start outside the Green Tree, the public house at Lake and West Water. Old settlers recalled Chester Ingersoll keeping it from 1834 to 1837.

choices.consequence: Light on the purse; the load rides on your back.
choices.label: A pack and straps — $3

choices.consequence: Dearer, but a hired wagon carries more than you can.
choices.label: Harness mended for a team — $6

stops.narrative: Settle first how the load will travel, or keep your money.
stops.text: A block west along Lake Street, at Canal, Goss and Cobb advertised saddles, harness, bridles and trunks in 1833. The partners parted in February 1835; Cobb's card says he will continue the business.

choices.consequence: Tires, hooks and chains looked over before the long road.
choices.label: Have the ironwork checked — $2

stops.narrative: Have the ironwork seen to before the long road, or trust it as it is.
stops.text: On the same crossing stands Asahel Pierce's smithy, opened in October 1833. Andreas records him ironing the first Chicago-to-St Louis stage line and making 'Bull' ploughs from 1834.

choices.consequence: Enough food for the first days on the road.
choices.label: Flour, pork and coffee — $5

stops.narrative: Stock up, or plan to buy along the way.
stops.text: Over the river on South Water, a Jones grocery and provision store advertised in 1833, and Andreas adds forwarding and commission by 1834. Neither source says where it stood; this position is reconstructed, and even Jones's initial is disputed.

choices.consequence: Hardware from the merchant's shelves, not the smith's forge.
choices.label: An axe and a few tools — $4

stops.narrative: Last on the list: tools for the road, or trust what you already own.
stops.text: A block east, Peck's store holds the corner of South Water and LaSalle. His own advertisements, from December 1833 through 1834, list dry goods, hardware, groceries, crockery, boots, shoes and hats.

title: Outfit for the West
